lessons.title: Lesson 1: Filming video you can actually use
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a phone to film usable game or practice video.
This lesson builds toward: Using a phone at a game or practice, you will film usable video from a high, central spot with a wide, steady view, with permission from your coach before filming and before sharing.
Good film starts with a good camera spot. Film from high up if you can, like the top of the bleachers, so you see the whole play and the spacing between players. Hold the phone sideways (landscape) and keep it steady with a tripod or by bracing it.
Follow the ball but keep enough of the field or court in view to see what players without the ball are doing. Do not zoom in too close.
Get permission. Your team, school or league may have rules about filming, and other people's children appear in youth sports video. Ask your coach before filming and before sharing anything.
Step by step:
- Ask your coach for permission to film.
- Find a high, central spot.
- Turn the phone sideways and steady it.
- Keep a wide view; follow the ball.
- Check battery and storage before the game.
Words to know:
- Landscape: holding the phone sideways, so the video is wide.
- Tripod: a three-legged stand that holds a camera steady.
Try it now: At your next practice, with your coach's okay, film five minutes from the highest spot you can find. Watch it back: can you see everyone involved in each play?
You can now set up a phone to film usable game or practice video, with permission.

check.q: Why keep a wide view instead of zooming in close?
options: To see what players without the ball are doing
check.why: A wide view shows spacing and players away from the ball.

check.q: You want to film your little sister's youth game and post it. What do you do first?
options: Post it and remove it if someone complains
Ask the coach about the rules before filming and sharing
check.why: Teams and leagues may have filming rules, and the video shows other people's children.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Watching film with a question
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick one clear question before you watch film.
This lesson builds toward: Before watching a game or practice film, you will write one narrow question and watch twice, pausing on plays that answer it, with one question per viewing and a short note for each linked play.
If you watch film with no plan, you mostly notice the highlights and your worst mistakes. Coaches watch with a question.
Good questions are narrow: "Where do I lose the ball?" "How fast do I get back on defense?" "Which serve receive lineups give up points?" "What does the other team do on third down?"
Pick one question per viewing. Watch once at normal speed for the big picture, then again and pause on each play that answers your question.
Step by step:
- Write one narrow question.
- Watch once at normal speed.
- Watch again and pause on each play linked to your question.
- Write a short note for each play.
Words to know:
- Film study: watching video of games or practice to learn and improve.
- Game intelligence: understanding why plays happen, not just what happened.
Try it now: Write three possible questions for your sport and position. Pick one and watch five minutes of film with it, writing a note each time it shows up.
You can now watch film with one clear question and take notes on the plays that answer it.

check.q: Which is a narrow film question?
options: How fast do I get back on defense?
check.why: Narrow questions point to specific plays you can pause and note.

check.q: You have two questions about your film. What do you do?
options: Ask AI to watch it instead
Watch with one question at a time

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Tagging plays in a spreadsheet
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Tag plays in Google Sheets so patterns can be counted.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sheets and your film, you will tag plays with Play #, Time, Situation, What happened, Result and Note, tagging at least 20 plays with the same tag words every time.
Tagging means writing the same few labels for each play. It turns video into data you can count.
Make columns: Play # , Time in video, Situation (for example "fast break" or "2nd and long"), What happened, Result (good, neutral or bad), and Note. Use the same words every time, so "turnover" is always "turnover", not sometimes "lost ball".
Team video apps such as Hudl tag plays for many schools; if your team uses one, ask your coach how to use its tags. A spreadsheet works for anyone, for free.
Step by step:
- Open Google Sheets.
- Columns: Play #, Time, Situation, What happened, Result, Note.
- Pick a short list of tag words and stick to them.
- Pause and fill one row per play.
- Tag at least 20 plays.
Words to know:
- Tag: a label you give each play, like "turnover" or "fast break".
- Timestamp: the time in the video where a play starts, like 12:45.
Try it now: Set up your tagging sheet and tag 10 plays from your film using your question from Lesson 2.
You can now tag plays in a spreadsheet with consistent labels and timestamps.

check.q: Which column records whether the play went well?
check.why: Result is good, neutral or bad.

check.q: You wrote "lost ball" for some plays and "turnover" for others. What do you do?
options: Change them all to one word, like "turnover"
Leave them; it does not matter
check.why: Using the same word every time keeps your counts correct.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Finding patterns and using them

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Counting patterns in your tags
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Count your tags and find the top patterns.
This lesson builds toward: Given at least 20 tagged plays, you will count your tags with sort, filter or COUNTIF and write the top two patterns with numbers, with any pattern based on only a few plays marked "watch more".
With 20 or more tagged plays, count how often each situation and result shows up. In Google Sheets you can sort by a column, use a filter, or use the COUNTIF formula to count a tag.
Look for patterns, not single plays: "7 of my 9 turnovers came when I dribbled left under pressure" is a pattern. One bad pass is not.
Small numbers can fool you. If something happened only twice, watch more film before you decide it is a real pattern.
Step by step:
- Sort or filter by Result.
- Count each Situation for bad results.
- Write the top two patterns as sentences with numbers.
- Mark any pattern with few plays as "watch more".
Words to know:
- Pattern: something that happens again and again in similar situations.
- COUNTIF: a spreadsheet formula that counts the cells that match a word or number.
Try it now: Finish tagging 20 plays. Count your results by situation and write your top two patterns as sentences with numbers.
You can now count tags and describe patterns with numbers.

check.q: Which of these is a pattern?
options: One bad pass in the second half
5 of my 6 missed shots came off the dribble
The best play of the game
check.why: A pattern repeats with numbers; one play is not a pattern.

check.q: A possible pattern shows up in only two plays. What do you do?
options: Build a whole practice around it
Tell the team it is your biggest problem
Mark it "watch more" and film more first
check.why: Small numbers can fool you, so watch more film before deciding.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Using AI to summarize your film notes
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask an AI assistant to summarize tagged plays and check its summary.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant and your tag table, you will ask for a summary of the top patterns with counts and check it against your own counts, with other players' names and private information removed and every count matching your sheet.
You can copy your tag table (no player names other than yours, and no private information) into an AI assistant and ask: "Here are my tagged plays. Summarize the top three patterns with counts, and suggest one question to ask my coach."
AI is good at spotting patterns in text tables, but it can miscount or invent things. Compare its counts with your own from the last lesson. If they differ, trust your sheet and fix the prompt.
Some AI tools can look at images or video, but they can misread fast sports action. Use your own tags as the main source and AI as a helper.
Step by step:
- Copy your tag table, removing other players' names and private info.
- Ask for the top three patterns with counts.
- Compare with your own counts.
- Fix any mistakes; your sheet wins.
Words to know:
- Summary: a short version that keeps the main points.
Try it now: Paste your 20 tagged plays into an AI assistant and ask for the top three patterns with counts. Check each count against your sheet.
You can now use AI to summarize film tags and check the summary against your own counts.

check.q: What can go wrong when AI summarizes your tag table?
options: It can miscount or invent things
check.why: AI can spot patterns but can miscount, so check it against your own counts.

check.q: Your tag table includes teammates' names. What do you do before pasting it into AI?
options: Remove other players' names and private information
Ask teammates to paste it instead
check.why: Keep other players' names and private information out of AI tools.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Turning film into a practice focus
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your top pattern into one practice focus agreed with your coach.
This lesson builds toward: Given your strongest pattern, you will write one practice focus and bring it to your coach with numbers, timestamps and a question, with the focus agreed with your coach and a plan to re-film and re-tag later.
Film only helps if it changes practice. Take your strongest pattern and turn it into one focus: "Protect the ball when pressured on my left side" or "Get back on defense within three seconds after a turnover."
Bring your coach the pattern, the numbers and two or three timestamps that show it. Ask: "What drill would help this?" Coaches love athletes who come with evidence and a question.
Film again in a few weeks and re-tag the same question to see if the pattern changed. That is game intelligence: learning, practicing and checking.
Step by step:
- Pick your strongest pattern.
- Write one practice focus.
- Pick two or three timestamps that show it.
- Ask your coach for a drill.
- Re-film and re-tag in a few weeks.
Words to know:
- Practice focus: one specific thing you work on in practice.
- Evidence: facts that show something is true, like counts and video timestamps.
Try it now: Final task: with your 20 tagged plays and AI summary, write one practice focus and pick two timestamps. Share it with your coach and ask for a drill.
You can now turn film patterns into a practice focus and check later whether it improved.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Film and permission Filmed without permission, or the video is too shaky or tight to see the play. Permission given, landscape video from a high spot with a wide, steady view. Battery and storage checked and the whole game or practice captured without gaps. Tag sheet Fewer than 20 plays, columns missing, or tag words change. At least 20 plays tagged in all six columns with the same tag words every time. Every row has a timestamp and a short note linked to the question. Patterns and AI check No counts, or the AI summary is used without checking. Top patterns written with counts and the AI's counts checked against the sheet, with names removed. Differences are found and the prompt is fixed; small-number patterns are marked "watch more". Practice focus No focus, or it is vague. One specific focus from the strongest pattern, reviewed with the coach using numbers and timestamps. A drill is agreed and a date set to re-film and re-tag the same question. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What makes a good practice focus?
options: One specific change from your strongest pattern
check.why: One focus from your strongest pattern changes practice.

check.q: Your coach suggests a drill for your focus. How do you check it worked?
options: Re-film in a few weeks and re-tag the same question
Ask the AI if it worked
check.why: Re-filming and re-tagging shows whether the pattern changed.
